newsitem.title: GERMANY: SAfrica sees global competition in stainless steel.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica sees global competition in stainless steel.

text.p: South Africa is looking to expand its exports of high-value stainless steel but has to address the harsh realities of global competition, said Fred Cawdry of the state's Industrial Development Corp (IDCSA).

South African plants were often finding it hard to compete in global markets with low-cost competitors such as India, Indonesia and China while the reduction of tariffs increased domestic import pressure, he said at a conference.
High input and operating costs hampered the country's efforts to move away from an emphasis of primary commodities exports in favour of downstream products with added value.
"But we do have a fairly advanced infrastructure, reliable upstream suppliers, confident management and attractive energy costs," he said.
Internal studies showed South African was competitive in stainless steel bulk transportation (containers) and tubular products but had little chance of succeeding in cookware.
Currently South Africa produces 580,000 tonnes of stainless steel of which it exports 500,000 tonnes, but after the full commissioning of new plants, this will rise dramatically.
Expansion in stainless steel output at the Columbus plant and two Iscor projects has caused a rapidly growing nickel demand, most of which has to be met by imports.
Columbus is a joint venture between Samancor Ltd, Highvel Steel and Vanadium Corp and the IDC.
Columbus, one of the biggest facilities in the world, and Iscor's plants plan to produce up to 1.2 million tonnes a year by the end of the decade, a Metal Bulletin publication said.

Nickel demand for this combined production could rise to nearly 75,000 tonnes per year (tpy) by then and over 50,000 tpy may need to be imported, unless domestic nickel reserves are successfully exploited, it said.
